To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
psychosocial factors, including depression and education, are more predictive of cognitive functioning than biomedical factors in end-stage renal disease patients.

1) the neurocognitive profile of ESRD patients is characterized by deficits in attentional processing and memory; 2) the neurocognition of ESRD is best described by a three factor model of sustained attention, focused attention, and memory recall; 3) the psychosocial and biological variables that are related to neurocognition are education, verbal skills, age, race/ethnicity, age by serum creatinine, serum creatinine, and type of renal replacement

(a) psychosocial variables are the best predictors of neurocognitive functioning in ESRD, and (b) the type of renal replacement modality is a statistically, but clinically not significant, predictor of neurocognitive function.

understanding the relationship between attention and memory and biomedical and psychosocial factors in patients with ESRD.
the development of an understanding of the neurocognitive deficits of patients with end-stage renal disease.

the development of a comprehensive model of the neurocognitive deficits of ESRD patients, and the identification of the factors that contribute to these deficits, with particular emphasis on the role of psychosocial variables.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

psychosocial factors (e.g., depression and education) and biomedical factors (e.g. age, renal replacement therapy, and creatinine levels) are important in the understanding of cognitive functioning in ESRD patients, but that the relationship between cognitive functioning and psychosocial factors is more important than the relationship between cognitive and biomedical variables.

we have demonstrated that psychosocial factors are the strongest predictors of cognitive performance in ESRD patients, and that type of renal replacement treatment is a statistically significant, but not clinically significant predictor of cognitive performance.
psychosocial factors, particularly depression, are more important predictors of attention and memory than biomedical factors in ESRD patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a strong link between focused attention and memory recall.
we can use the results of the study to develop interventions to improve attention and memory in patients with kidney failure.
we have to do more to understand the cognitive and psychosocial factors that contribute to the poor outcomes of patients on dialysis.
